title: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
summary: Learn what survives sampling, why the DFT is a change of basis into sinusoids, how bins and windows shape a spectrum, how the FFT gets to N log N, and how FIR and IIR filters clean real sensor data.
outcomes: Explain aliasing and compute where a frequency above fs/2 appears after sampling
Compute a small DFT by hand as dot products with cosine and sine basis vectors
Explain frequency resolution, spectral leakage and the resolution vs leakage trade-off of windows
Explain how the FFT's butterflies reduce N squared work to N log N
Choose between moving average, FIR, IIR and zero-phase filtering for a sensor task

lessons.title: Sampling: why a 7 Hz wave sampled at 10 Hz looks like 3 Hz

blocks.md: A sensor does not hand you a continuous curve. An accelerometer, microphone or power meter measures the signal once every $\Delta t$ seconds and gives you a list of numbers. The **sampling rate** is $f_s = 1/\Delta t$ samples per second (Hz). Every tool in this course (spectra, filters, the FFT) works on that list, so the first question is what the list can and cannot tell you.

Half the sampling rate, $f_s/2$, is called the **Nyquist frequency**. The **sampling theorem** (Nyquist and Shannon) says a continuous signal can be reconstructed exactly from its samples if it contains no frequencies above $f_s/2$. Steven W. Smith's *Scientist and Engineer's Guide to DSP* states it this way and warns that the names "Nyquist frequency" and "Nyquist rate" are used inconsistently, so always say which number you mean.

blocks.prompt: A 7 Hz cosine is sampled at 10 Hz for one second (10 samples). You run `np.fft.rfft` on those 10 samples and look for the biggest peak. At which frequency is it?
blocks.reveal: The peak is at **3 Hz** (bin 3 of the 6 bins 0, 1, ..., 5 Hz), with height 5 and every other bin 0. Nothing in the data says 7 Hz. The 10 samples of the 7 Hz cosine are identical to the samples of a 3 Hz cosine: our script finds a largest difference of about $3 \times 10^{-15}$, which is floating point rounding.

blocks.title: Two different waves, the same ten samples

scenes.caption: The true signal is a 7 Hz cosine. The dots are its samples every 0.1 s: 1, -0.31, -0.81, 0.81, 0.31, -1, and so on.
A 3 Hz cosine passes through every one of the same dots. Between samples the waves differ, but the samples never see that.
Given only the dots, the simplest explanation below the 5 Hz Nyquist frequency is 3 Hz. That is aliasing: the 7 Hz wave has taken on a 3 Hz identity.

blocks.md:
The general rule: a frequency $f$ sampled at $f_s$ shows up at the distance from $f$ to the nearest whole multiple of $f_s$. For $f_s = 10$ Hz:

- 1, 3, 5 Hz stay as they are (at or below 5 Hz)
- 7 Hz shows as 3 Hz, 9 Hz as 1 Hz
- 11 Hz as 1 Hz, 13 Hz as 3 Hz, 17 Hz as 3 Hz, 23 Hz as 3 Hz

Smith notes that aliasing can also flip the phase: the samples of a 7 Hz *sine* at 10 Hz equal the samples of a 3 Hz sine multiplied by -1.

blocks.caption: Folding rule for a real sinusoid of frequency f sampled at rate f_s. The result always lies between 0 and f_s/2.

blocks.title: The folding zigzag: true frequency vs what you measure

scenes.caption: At fs = 10 Hz the line climbs to 5 Hz (fs/2), then folds back down. Read the curve at the 7 Hz line: it shows 3 Hz.
At fs = 8 Hz, 7 Hz sits just below 8, so it folds all the way down to 1 Hz. Lower sampling rates fold more of the spectrum.
At fs = 20 Hz the Nyquist frequency is 10 Hz, so 7 Hz is measured correctly. Drag the slider: anything right of the fs/2 line folds back.

blocks.md: Aliasing cannot be undone after sampling: once 7 Hz and 3 Hz produce the same numbers, no algorithm can tell them apart. Remove content above $f_s/2$ *before* sampling (an analog anti-aliasing filter) or before you downsample. SciPy's `scipy.signal.decimate` does this for you: it applies an anti-aliasing filter (by default an order 8 Chebyshev type I) before keeping every q-th sample.
Frequencies above $f_s/2$ do not disappear when you sample. They fold into the range 0 to $f_s/2$ and pretend to be something else.

blocks.question: A vibration sensor samples at 100 Hz. A motor nearby vibrates at 130 Hz. Where does the motor appear in your spectrum?
options: Nowhere: it is above 50 Hz, so it is filtered out by sampling
At 130 Hz, beyond the last bin
At 30 Hz
At 50 Hz, piled up at the Nyquist frequency
blocks.explain: 130 Hz is 30 Hz away from the nearest multiple of 100 Hz (which is 100), so it folds to 30 Hz. Sampling is not a filter: energy above fs/2 is not removed, it is relabeled. This is why sensors need an anti-aliasing filter before the converter.

blocks.question: You have 1000 Hz sensor data and want 100 Hz. A colleague writes `y = x[::10]`. What is the problem?
options: Nothing: keeping every 10th sample is exactly what downsampling means
Content between 50 and 500 Hz folds into the 0 to 50 Hz band, because nothing removed it first
The result has the wrong length; it should be `x[::100]`
Slicing shifts the phase by half a sample, which is the only error
blocks.explain: Keeping every 10th sample makes the new Nyquist frequency 50 Hz. Anything in the original data between 50 and 500 Hz now aliases into 0 to 50 Hz. Low-pass filter first, or use `scipy.signal.decimate(x, 10)`, which filters then downsamples.

lessons.title: The DFT: one dot product per complex sinusoid

blocks.md: From the linear algebra prerequisite: if the basis vectors are orthogonal, the coordinate of a vector along one basis vector is just a dot product (divided by that basis vector's squared length). The **discrete Fourier transform (DFT)** is exactly this, using sampled sinusoids as the basis. For $N$ samples there are $N$ basis vectors, one per frequency $k = 0, 1, \dots, N-1$, where frequency $k$ means $k$ whole cycles across the $N$ samples.

blocks.tex: X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n]\, e^{-2\pi i k n / N} = \sum_{n} x[n] \cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi k n}{N}\right) \; - \; i \sum_{n} x[n] \sin\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi k n}{N}\right)
blocks.caption: The DFT as NumPy defines it. The real part is a dot product with a cosine, the imaginary part a dot product with a negative sine.

blocks.md: A toy signal with $N = 8$: $x = [1, 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0]$. It is $1 + \sin(2\pi \cdot 2n/8)$: a constant 1 plus a sine that makes 2 full cycles over the 8 samples. Let us compute its DFT by hand, one row of the DFT matrix at a time. Row $k$ of the cosine matrix holds $\cos(2\pi k n / 8)$ for $n = 0..7$, and $0.71$ is $\sqrt{2}/2$ rounded.

blocks.title: The 8-point DFT matrix, row by row

scenes.caption: Real part of the DFT matrix: row k is a cosine with k cycles across 8 samples. Row 0 is all ones; row 4 alternates +1, -1 (the fastest wave 8 samples can show).
Row 0 dot x = 1+2+1+0+1+2+1+0 = 8. That is the sum of the signal, so X[0]/N = 1 is its mean.
Row 1 dot x: the terms are 1, 1.41, 0, 0, -1, -1.41, 0, 0, which cancel to 0. x has no 1-cycle component.
Row 2 (cosine, 2 cycles) dot x: 1 + 0 - 1 + 0 + 1 + 0 - 1 + 0 = 0. The 2-cycle part of x is a sine, so the cosine misses it.
Now the imaginary part, -sin(2 pi k n / 8). Row 2 dot x: only n=1 and n=5 are nonzero, giving -2 + -2 = -4. So X[2] = 0 - 4i.
Row 6 of the sine part gives +4, so X[6] = +4i, the complex conjugate of X[2]. Apart from cosine row 0, every other row of both matrices dots to 0.

blocks.title: Magnitude |X[k]| as the rows are computed

scenes.caption: After row 0: X[0] = 8 (the constant).
After row 2: |X[2]| = |-4i| = 4 (the 2-cycle sine).
All 8 rows: |X| = [8, 0, 4, 0, 0, 0, 4, 0]. np.fft.fft(x) returns the same numbers.

blocks.md:
Reading the result:

- **Mean**: $X[0]/N = 8/8 = 1$.
- **Amplitude** of the sinusoid in bin $k$ (for $0 < k < N/2$): $2|X[k]|/N = 2 \cdot 4 / 8 = 1$, the amplitude of our sine.
- **Phase**: $X[2] = -4i$ is purely imaginary, which says sine, not cosine.
- **Mirror**: bin 6 is really frequency $-2$ (NumPy's `fftfreq` lists bins $N/2+1$ to $N-1$ as negative frequencies). For real input $X[N-k]$ is the complex conjugate of $X[k]$, so `np.fft.rfft` returns only the $N/2 + 1 = 5$ non-negative bins.

blocks.tex: F_{kn} = e^{-2\pi i k n / N}, \qquad F F^{H} = N I, \qquad x = \tfrac{1}{N} F^{H} X
blocks.caption: The rows of F are orthogonal, each with squared length N. So the inverse DFT is the conjugate transpose divided by N: a change of basis and back, with nothing lost.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
N = 8
n = np.arange(N)
x = 1 + np.sin(2 * np.pi * 2 * n / N)       # [1, 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0]
F = np.exp(-2j * np.pi * np.outer(n, n) / N)  # DFT matrix
X = F @ x                                     # 8 dot products
print(np.round(X, 6))       # [8, 0, -4j, 0, 0, 0, 4j, 0]
print(np.allclose(X, np.fft.fft(x)))          # True
print(np.allclose(F @ F.conj().T, N * np.eye(N)))  # True: orthogonal rows
print(np.round(np.fft.rfft(x), 6))  # [8, 0, -4j, 0, 0] (non-negative bins)
blocks.caption: Every number in this lesson, checked with NumPy.

blocks.md: The DFT is a matrix-vector product: $N$ dot products of the signal with orthogonal complex sinusoids. Each $X[k]$ says how much of frequency $k$ is present (magnitude) and where it starts (phase), and the inverse DFT rebuilds $x$ exactly.

blocks.question: x is a real signal of length 8 and its DFT has X[3] = 2 + 5i. What is X[5]?
options: 0, because only one of a pair can be nonzero
blocks.explain: For real input, X[N - k] is the complex conjugate of X[k]. Here N - 3 = 5, so X[5] = 2 - 5i. This symmetry is why rfft can skip the upper half of the bins without losing information.

blocks.question: In the toy example, the cosine row k=2 dotted with x gave exactly 0 even though x clearly has a 2-cycle component. Why?
options: The 2-cycle part of x is a sine, which is orthogonal to the 2-cycle cosine; the sine row picks it up instead
The DFT can only detect cosines, so the sine is lost
Rounding 0.71 to two decimals cancelled the sum
Bin 2 is above the Nyquist frequency for 8 samples
blocks.explain: Over a whole number of cycles, a sine and a cosine of the same frequency are orthogonal. That is why each bin needs two dot products (or one complex one): the cosine part measures the in-phase component, the sine part the quadrature component. Together they give magnitude 4 and phase.

lessons.title: Frequency bins, resolution and spectral leakage

blocks.md: Bin $k$ corresponds to the frequency $k \cdot f_s / N$ Hz. The spacing between bins, the **frequency resolution**, is $\Delta f = f_s / N = 1 / (N \Delta t)$, which is one over the duration of the recording. Example: $N = 32$ samples at $f_s = 32$ Hz is one second of data, so the bins sit at 0, 1, 2, ..., 16 Hz (17 bins from `rfft`).

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
fs, N = 32, 32
print(np.fft.rfftfreq(N, d=1/fs))   # [0. 1. 2. ... 16.]  17 bins, 1 Hz apart
print(fs / N)                         # 1.0 Hz resolution = 1 / (1 second)
blocks.caption: `rfftfreq(n, d)` takes the sample spacing d = 1/fs and returns bin centers in Hz.

blocks.prompt: A 4 Hz cosine sampled for exactly 1 s gives a single nonzero bin at 4 Hz. Now use a 4.5 Hz cosine instead, halfway between bins 4 and 5. What do you expect the spectrum to look like?
blocks.reveal: Not two neat half-height bars. The energy smears across **every** bin: bins 4 and 5 are at 0.92 and 1.00 of the peak, but even bin 0 is at 0.09 and bin 12 is only 19.4 dB below the peak. This smearing is called **spectral leakage**.

blocks.title: Leakage with and without a Hann window (N = 32, fs = 32 Hz)

scenes.caption: 4 Hz cosine, no window: exactly 4 cycles fit in the 32 samples, so it matches basis vector k=4 and every other bin is 0.
4.5 Hz cosine, no window: 4.5 cycles do not fit. Energy leaks into every bin, from 0.09 at 0 Hz to 0.15 at 9 Hz (normalized to the peak).
Same 4.5 Hz signal times a Hann window: far bins collapse (0.004 at 9 Hz; bin 12 drops from -19.4 dB to -61.2 dB). Near bins 3 and 6 still hold 0.20.
The price: an on-bin 4 Hz cosine with a Hann window now covers three bins (0.5, 1, 0.5). The window widens the peak, so close tones are harder to separate.

blocks.md: Why leakage happens: the DFT basis only contains sinusoids that complete a whole number of cycles in $N$ samples. A 4.5 Hz tone is not any one of them, so its dot product with *every* basis vector is nonzero. Another view, from Smith's chapter on DFT applications: taking a finite block multiplies the endless signal by a rectangular window, and that sudden cut at both ends spreads a sharp peak into a peak with long tails.

A **window** fixes the cut by fading the block in and out. The Hann window is $w[n] = 0.5 - 0.5\cos(2\pi n / N)$, which starts at 0, peaks at 1 in the middle and falls back toward 0 at the end (this is the periodic form, used here). Multiply the samples by $w$, then take the FFT. Two side effects, both visible above: the main peak gets wider (resolution gets worse), and the peak height scales by the window's mean, $\sum w / N = 16/32 = 0.5$ here. Smith summarizes the choice of window as a trade-off between resolution (peak width) and spectral leakage (tail height).

Zero-padding does not improve resolution. Smith: padding a 256-point signal to 2048 points gives 1025 spectrum samples, but "the added zeros don't change the shape of the spectrum, they only provide more samples in the frequency domain." To separate two close frequencies you need a longer *recording*.

In SciPy, `scipy.signal.windows.hann(M, sym=True)` is the default symmetric window meant for filter design. For spectral analysis the docs recommend the periodic version, `sym=False`, which is what this lesson uses.

blocks.question: You record 2 s of data at 1000 Hz and need to tell apart tones at 50.0 Hz and 50.3 Hz. What helps?
options: Zero-pad to 8 times the length before the FFT
Sample at 4000 Hz instead of 1000 Hz for the same 2 s
Record for longer: at least several seconds, since the bin spacing is 1/duration
Apply a Hann window, which sharpens peaks
blocks.explain: Resolution is fs/N = 1/duration. Two seconds gives 0.5 Hz bins, too coarse for a 0.3 Hz gap; you need more than 1/0.3 = 3.3 s, and more still with a window, which widens peaks. A higher fs adds bins at high frequencies but keeps the spacing at 1/duration. Zero-padding only interpolates the same blurred spectrum.

blocks.question: Audio at 48000 Hz is analyzed with a 4096-point FFT. What is the spacing between frequency bins?
options: About 11.7 Hz
About 0.085 Hz
blocks.explain: Bin spacing is fs/N = 48000/4096 = 11.71875 Hz. 24000 Hz is the Nyquist frequency (the last rfft bin), not the spacing. A 4096-sample block lasts about 85 ms, and the spacing is the inverse of that duration.

lessons.title: The FFT: from N squared to N log N with butterflies

blocks.md: Computed directly, the DFT does $N$ dot products of length $N$: about $N^2$ complex multiply-adds. For $N = 1024$ that is 1,048,576. Smith timed this on a 100 MHz Pentium: a 1024-point DFT by correlation took about 25 seconds, while the **fast Fourier transform (FFT)** took about 70 ms, over 300 times faster. The FFT computes exactly the same $X[k]$; it just reorganizes the arithmetic.

J. W. Cooley and J. W. Tukey published the algorithm in 1965 ("An algorithm for the machine calculation of complex Fourier series", *Mathematics of Computation* 19, pp. 297 to 301). Both Smith and the NumPy docs note that Gauss knew the method much earlier; it became important when digital computers made it practical.

The trick (radix-2, decimation in time): split $x$ into its even-indexed and odd-indexed samples. Each half is a signal of length $N/2$ with its own DFT, $E$ and $O$. Every output of the full DFT is then one **butterfly**: a sum and a difference of $E[k]$ and a rotated $O[k]$. Apply the split recursively and you get $\log_2 N$ stages of $N/2$ butterflies each.

blocks.tex: X[k] = E[k] + W^{k} O[k], \qquad X[k + N/2] = E[k] - W^{k} O[k], \qquad W = e^{-2\pi i / N}, \; k = 0, \dots, N/2 - 1
blocks.caption: One butterfly produces two outputs from two inputs with one complex multiplication by the twiddle factor W^k.

scenes.caption: Inputs are reordered into evens (x0, x2) and odds (x1, x3). For larger N this reordering is the bit reversal sort Smith describes.
Stage 1: two 2-point DFTs, each a sum and a difference. E = [1+1, 1-1] = [2, 0] and O = [2+0, 2-0] = [2, 2].
Stage 2, first butterfly (W^0 = 1): X0 = E0 + O0 = 4 and X2 = E0 - O0 = 0.
Second butterfly (W^1 = -i): X1 = 0 + (-i)(2) = -2i and X3 = 0 - (-i)(2) = 2i. Result [4, -2i, 0, 2i] matches np.fft.fft([1, 2, 1, 0]).

blocks.title: Complex multiplications: direct DFT vs radix-2 FFT

scenes.caption: Simplified count (multiplications only): the direct DFT grows as N squared, a straight line of slope 2 on log-log axes.
The FFT needs (N/2) log2 N twiddle multiplications. At N = 1024 that is 5,120 vs 1,048,576 (205x); at N = 4096, 24,576 vs 16,777,216 (683x).

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

def fft(a):
    a = np.asarray(a, dtype=complex)
    N = len(a)                      # N must be a power of two here
    if N == 1:
        return a
    E = fft(a[0::2])                # DFT of even samples
    O = fft(a[1::2])                # DFT of odd samples
    W = np.exp(-2j * np.pi * np.arange(N // 2) / N)
    return np.concatenate([E + W * O, E - W * O])   # N/2 butterflies

x = np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal(1024)
print(np.allclose(fft(x), np.fft.fft(x)))   # True
blocks.caption: A textbook recursive radix-2 FFT. Library FFTs are iterative and heavily optimized, but compute the same thing.

blocks.prompt: You double N from 1024 to 2048. Roughly how much more work does the direct DFT do, and how much more does the FFT do?
blocks.reveal: The direct DFT does **4x** the work ($N^2$). The FFT does $2048 \cdot 11 / (1024 \cdot 10) = $ **2.2x** the work: one more stage, and twice as many butterflies per stage. This is why Smith calls the FFT important for small N and "absolutely critical" for N of 1024 and above.

blocks.md: The FFT is not an approximation. It returns the same numbers as the DFT matrix product, up to floating point rounding, by sharing work through $\log_2 N$ stages of $N/2$ butterflies.

blocks.question: How many butterflies does a radix-2 FFT of N = 8 samples perform?
blocks.explain: There are log2 8 = 3 stages and each stage has N/2 = 4 butterflies, so 12 in total. 64 is the number of multiply-adds in the direct DFT (N squared), and 24 is N log2 N, which counts outputs over all stages (8 per stage), two per butterfly.

lessons.title: Convolution, the convolution theorem and FIR filters

blocks.md: A **filter** turns an input signal into an output signal. The simplest useful kind is a **finite impulse response (FIR)** filter: each output is a weighted sum of the last few inputs. The weights $h$ are called the **kernel** or **impulse response** (feed in a single 1 and the output is $h$). The operation is **convolution**, written $y = x * h$.

blocks.tex: y[n] = \sum_{j=0}^{M-1} h[j]\, x[n - j], \qquad \text{moving average: } h[j] = \tfrac{1}{M}
blocks.caption: Each output is a dot product of the kernel with a sliding window of the input.

blocks.title: A 3-point moving average sliding along a signal

scenes.caption: The input has a block of 3s (a step up and down) and a single spike of 6 (one bad sensor reading). Each output averages x at i-1, i, i+1 (centered, like mode='same').
At i = 1 the window holds 0, 0, 3, so y[1] = 1. The output starts to rise one sample before the step.
At i = 3 the window is 3, 3, 3, so y[3] = 3. Inside the flat block the average leaves the value unchanged.
At i = 7 the window is 0, 6, 0, so y[7] = 2. The spike of 6 is cut to a third of its height, and spread to i = 6, 7, 8.
Final output [0, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 0]: noise spikes shrink, but the sharp step edges become ramps. Smoothing always trades noise for edge sharpness.

blocks.md: Smith's *Guide* gives the moving average a strong endorsement: for reducing random white noise while keeping the sharpest step response, no linear filter does better. Noise falls by the square root of $M$. Checking with NumPy on unit-variance random noise, averaging 4, 9, 25 and 100 points leaves a standard deviation of 0.49, 0.33, 0.20 and 0.098, matching $1/\sqrt{M}$.

The **convolution theorem** links this to the previous lessons: convolution in time is multiplication in frequency. The spectrum of the output is the spectrum of the input times the filter's **frequency response** $H$ (the DFT of the kernel). So a filter's effect on each frequency is just a gain, $|H(f)|$, and the FFT gives a fast way to convolve long signals.

blocks.tex: y = x * h \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad Y[k] = X[k] \cdot H[k]
blocks.caption: For the DFT this product gives circular convolution. Zero-pad both signals to length at least N + M - 1 to get ordinary (linear) convolution.

blocks.md: Multiplying two N-point FFTs and inverting gives *circular* convolution: the end of the output wraps around onto the start. Zero-pad first. In the toy above, padding both to 10 + 3 - 1 = 12 points makes `ifft(fft(x, 12) * fft(h, 12))` match `np.convolve(x, h)` exactly.
What does the moving average do to each frequency? Its frequency response (Smith, Eq. 15-2), with $f$ in cycles per sample from 0 to 0.5:

blocks.title: Moving average frequency response: drag M

scenes.caption: M = 3: gain 0.87 at f = 0.1, a null at f = 1/3, then a bump back up to 0.33 at Nyquist. A low-pass shape, but a leaky one.
M = 5: gain 0.65 at f = 0.1 and nulls at f = 0.2 and 0.4. The nulls sit at multiples of 1/M.
M = 11: the main lobe narrows, but the first side lobe still reaches 0.22. Smith: slow roll-off, "ghastly" stopband. Great smoother, bad frequency separator.

blocks.md: To actually separate frequency bands, use a filter designed in the frequency domain. `scipy.signal.firwin(numtaps, cutoff, fs=...)` designs an FIR low-pass by the window method (a windowed sinc, default window `'hamming'`). Its result has linear phase (every frequency is delayed by the same amount), and `cutoff` is the half-amplitude point, about -6 dB. Below, both filters run at $f_s = 100$ Hz with a 10 Hz target.

blocks.title: Gain per frequency at fs = 100 Hz: moving average vs firwin

scenes.caption: 10-point moving average: a null at 10 Hz, but 0.22 of a 15 Hz signal passes, and 0.10 even at 45 Hz. It also already cuts 5 Hz to 0.64.
31-tap firwin low-pass, cutoff 10 Hz: 0.99 at 5 Hz, 0.50 at the 10 Hz cutoff, 0.009 at 15 Hz, about 0.001 or less above that.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import signal
fs = 100
taps = signal.firwin(31, 10, fs=fs)          # 31-tap low-pass, cutoff 10 Hz
f, H = signal.freqz(taps, worN=[5, 10, 15], fs=fs)
print(np.round(abs(H), 3))                    # [0.989 0.498 0.009]
y = signal.lfilter(taps, 1.0, x)              # apply: plain convolution
# delay of a linear-phase FIR is (numtaps - 1) / 2 = 15 samples
blocks.caption: Assumes x is your 100 Hz signal. `freqz` evaluates a filter's frequency response.

blocks.question: A temperature sensor has occasional random noise and you must keep step changes (a door opening) as sharp as possible. Which filter fits best?
options: A short moving average
A 101-tap firwin low-pass with a very sharp cutoff
An FFT, zeroing all bins above a cutoff, then an inverse FFT
No filter: any averaging destroys steps
blocks.explain: This is the job Smith says the moving average is optimal for: least noise for a given edge sharpness. Sharp frequency-domain filters have long kernels that ring around steps. Use firwin-style filters when the goal is separating frequency bands, not smoothing in time.

blocks.question: You compute `ifft(fft(x) * fft(h, len(x)))` to convolve a 1000-sample signal with a 50-tap kernel, and the first 49 output samples look wrong. Why?
options: The FFT is only approximate for lengths that are not powers of two
The DFT product gives circular convolution, so the tail of the output wrapped around onto the start
The kernel must be reversed before the FFT
fft(h, len(x)) truncates the kernel
blocks.explain: Multiplying DFTs is circular convolution. The full linear result has 1000 + 50 - 1 = 1049 samples; with only 1000 bins the last 49 wrap onto the first 49. Zero-pad both to at least 1049 (scipy.signal.fftconvolve does this for you).

lessons.title: IIR filters, zero-phase filtering and real sensor data

blocks.md: An FIR filter only looks at inputs. A **recursive** filter also feeds back its own past outputs. Smith's simplest example, the single pole low-pass, has two coefficients: $y[n] = a_0 x[n] + b_1 y[n-1]$, with $a_0 = 1 - d$ and $b_1 = d$, where the decay $d$ between 0 and 1 (Smith calls it $x$) is the fraction of the output kept per sample. Because the feedback never fully stops, the impulse response decays forever: these are **infinite impulse response (IIR)** filters.

blocks.title: Single pole low-pass with decay x = 0.8, fed an impulse
blocks.code:
decay = 0.8
a0, b1 = 1 - decay, decay
y_prev = 0.0
for n, xn in enumerate([1, 0, 0, 0, 0]):
    y = a0 * xn + b1 * y_prev
    y_prev = y
    print(n, round(y, 5))

scenes.caption: Two coefficients: a0 = 0.2 scales the new input, b1 = 0.8 carries the previous output forward.
n = 0: the impulse arrives. y = 0.2 x 1 + 0.8 x 0 = 0.2.
n = 1: input is 0 now, but feedback keeps the output alive: y = 0.8 x 0.2 = 0.16.
Each step multiplies by 0.8: 0.128, 0.1024, 0.08192. The response never reaches exactly zero, which is what infinite impulse response means.

blocks.md: Why bother: recursion gets a long effective response from a handful of coefficients, so IIR filters are cheap. The cost is that their phase response is not linear (different frequencies are delayed by different amounts) and, with badly chosen coefficients, feedback can make them unstable. A standard design is the **Butterworth** filter, which SciPy describes as having a maximally flat passband. `scipy.signal.butter(N, Wn, fs=...)` designs an order N filter whose gain at `Wn` is $1/\sqrt{2}$ (the -3 dB point).

A 4th-order Butterworth low-pass at 5 Hz for 100 Hz data, evaluated with `sosfreqz`: gain 1.000 at 1 Hz, 0.998 at 2.5 Hz, 0.707 at 5 Hz, 0.056 at 10 Hz and 0.002 at 20 Hz. Compare the 10-point moving average, which still passed 0.22 at 15 Hz.

Ask SciPy for second-order sections: `butter(..., output='sos')`, then `sosfilt` or `sosfiltfilt`. The default `output='ba'` returns polynomial coefficients, and the SciPy docs warn that the conversion is numerically sensitive "even for N >= 4" and that high-order or narrowband designs in that form can filter incorrectly. Also note: without `fs`, `Wn` is a fraction of the Nyquist frequency, so `butter(4, 0.1)` means 5 Hz for 100 Hz data.

Causal filters (those that only use past samples) always delay the signal. Offline you can avoid that: `filtfilt` and `sosfiltfilt` run the filter forward, then backward over the result. The SciPy docs: the combined filter has **zero phase** and twice the original order. The experiment below uses a 1.5 Hz sine sampled at 100 Hz for 10 s, plus Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.5 (seed 42), and measures RMS error against the clean sine.

blocks.prompt: Will the causal Butterworth filter (`sosfilt`) lower the RMS error against the clean sine, compared with doing nothing?
blocks.reveal: No. It removes most of the noise but delays the sine by about 8 samples (80 ms), and that shift alone makes its error **0.557**, worse than the raw data's 0.495. Running the same filter forward and backward with `sosfiltfilt` removes the delay and gets **0.158**.

blocks.title: Denoising a 1.5 Hz sine: RMS error vs the clean signal

scenes.caption: Raw samples: RMS error 0.495, essentially the noise level of 0.5.
A centered 9-point moving average (mode='same', so no delay): 0.175.
4th-order 5 Hz Butterworth, causal: 0.557. The noise is gone but the output lags by 8 samples, so it misses the clean sine everywhere.
Same filter forward and backward (sosfiltfilt): 0.158, the best of the four, with zero phase shift. It needs the whole signal, so it is for offline use.

blocks.md: The other everyday use is **detecting periodicity**: a heart rate, a gait cadence, a machine's rotation speed. Toy setup: a 1.5 Hz sine of amplitude 0.5 buried in noise of standard deviation 1.0 (seed 7), 20 s at 50 Hz, so $N = 1000$ and bins are $50/1000 = 0.05$ Hz apart. Subtract the mean, apply a Hann window, take `rfft`, and look for peaks. The median bin magnitude is 14.7.

blocks.title: Spectrum magnitude at selected frequencies (Hann window, N = 1000)

scenes.caption: In the time domain the sine is hard to see. In the spectrum the 1.5 Hz bin stands at 111.7, about 7.6 times the median bin (14.7).
`scipy.signal.find_peaks(mag, height=5 * median)` returns exactly one peak: 1.5 Hz. The noise is spread over all 501 bins; the sine is concentrated in a few.
Lesson 1: filter away content above the new Nyquist frequency before reducing the rate; scipy.signal.decimate bundles both steps.
Lessons 5 and 6: smooth with a moving average or a Butterworth filter; use sosfiltfilt offline for zero phase, a causal filter for real-time use.
Lessons 2 to 4: window the block, take the FFT, and read features (dominant frequency, band energy) from the bins.

blocks.md: Pick the filter by the job: moving average to smooth in time, windowed-sinc FIR (firwin) for clean band separation with linear phase, Butterworth IIR (as SOS) for a cheap sharp cutoff. Offline, filter forward and backward to cancel the delay.

blocks.question: A drone's control loop needs a filtered gyro reading every 1 ms. Someone proposes `sosfiltfilt` because it has zero phase delay. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; zero phase is ideal for control
sosfiltfilt only works on FIR filters
sosfiltfilt runs the filter backward from the end of the signal, so it needs future samples and cannot run in real time
sosfiltfilt halves the filter order, so it filters too weakly
blocks.explain: The backward pass starts from the last sample, which a real-time loop does not have yet. Real-time systems must use a causal filter (sosfilt, or an FIR) and accept or compensate its delay. Forward-backward filtering doubles the effective order; it does not halve it.

blocks.question: A 20 s recording at 50 Hz shows a spectral peak at 1.5 Hz. The bins are 0.05 Hz apart. A colleague wants 0.01 Hz precision on the rate. What is the honest way to get finer frequency resolution?
options: Record a longer segment (100 s gives 0.01 Hz bins)
Raise the sampling rate to 250 Hz
Zero-pad to 5000 samples, which gives true 0.01 Hz resolution
Use a causal Butterworth filter before the FFT
blocks.explain: Resolution is 1/duration, so 0.01 Hz needs about 100 s of data. A higher fs only extends the frequency range. Zero-padding interpolates between bins (useful to locate a single clean peak more precisely) but does not separate close frequencies, as Smith points out.
